title: How can a house express a community's life?
essentialQuestion: How can a house express a community's life?
learningGoal: Describe how a building's materials and construction fit together, explain how a house can carry family, cultural and social meaning, and tell what a photograph shows from what other sources explain.

evidence.question: Toraja communities in the highlands of South Sulawesi, Indonesia; inherited settlement traditions and buildings photographed in 2011 and 2014. Look at each whole building first, then at its roof, supports and carving.

sections.heading: Houses contain more than rooms
sections.text:
A house gives people a place to live, but its design can also express relationships between people. Rooms, materials and decoration may reflect work, family connections, beliefs and the resources people had. A photograph shows some features. To understand what they mean, we also need to know about the community and the particular building.

In South Sulawesi, Indonesia, tongkonan are ancestral houses linked with Toraja communities. Ancestral means connected with earlier generations of a family or community. Raised floors, timber frames and curved roofs make these houses easy to recognise. Yet they belong to a larger setting. Indonesia's description of traditional Toraja settlements includes houses, granaries (buildings for storing rice), farmland and places for the community and its ceremonies. Different settlements keep different mixes of these. There is no identical village repeated everywhere.

This is a highland setting on Sulawesi. It is a different island from Java, where the batiks in Lesson 2 were made. Village life connected rice fields and granaries with spaces for family gatherings and ceremonies. At Nanggala, houses and granaries face each other across an open space where people gather. This shows why a roof alone is not the whole architecture. Architecture is the design and building of places, and the way buildings relate to each other also helps organise a community's life. A Toraja example should not stand for all housing in Indonesia.
sections.simpler:
A house is a place to live. But its design can also show how people are connected. Rooms, materials and decoration can show work, family and beliefs. A photo shows some things. To know what they mean, we need to learn about the people and the place.

In South Sulawesi, Indonesia, Toraja communities have houses called tongkonan. They are ancestral houses. Ancestral means linked to earlier generations of a family. They have raised floors, wooden frames and curved roofs. But a house is part of a bigger place. A Toraja village can have houses, rice stores, fields and places for ceremonies. Each village is different.

Sulawesi is a different island from Java. Java is where the batiks in Lesson 2 were made. At Nanggala, houses and rice stores face each other across an open space. People gather there. So a roof is not the whole story. Architecture is the design of buildings and places. How buildings sit together is part of it too. One Toraja village does not stand for all homes in Indonesia.

sections.heading: Family, meaning and carving
sections.text:
Indonesia's national museum, the Museum Nasional Indonesia, explains that a tongkonan is connected with family discussion and customary affairs. These are matters guided by a community's long-standing rules. The museum's account describes three parts: the area below the floor, the main living space and the roof. These parts can carry cultural meanings as well as practical uses. So architecture organises social life, not simply empty space indoors.

Carving also matters. The museum describes decorated walls, doors, windows and roof supports. It explains that some motifs, or repeated designs, relate to social standing and customary rules. Ornament here is decoration that can also carry meaning. It would be wrong to assume that every design is only decoration, or that every house may use every motif. We can describe a carved pattern from a photograph. But we should not invent its meaning because it looks like something familiar to us. Family relationships and differences in status matter to the explanation.
sections.simpler:
Indonesia's national museum says a tongkonan is linked to family talks and customary matters. These are things decided by a community's old rules. The museum describes three parts. There is the space under the floor, the main living space and the roof. Each part can have a meaning as well as a use. So a building helps organise how people live together.

Carving matters too. Walls, doors, windows and roof supports are carved. The museum says some designs are linked to a family's rank and to community rules. This kind of ornament is decoration with a meaning. Not every house may use every design. We can describe a carved pattern from a photo. But we should not guess its meaning just because it looks familiar.

sections.heading: Particular buildings and a living heritage
sections.text:
The two photographs show particular buildings in the Toraja region at particular times. They let us notice roofs, repeated forms and the supports that make up each building's structure. We can also see how the buildings stand in relation to each other. The photographs do not tell us who lived in every room, or what all Toraja people believe today. An ancestral house can carry shared importance without being a complete picture of family life today.

Heritage is living. People look after buildings, replace materials, change spaces and decide how traditions continue. Living heritage means inherited practices and places that people still use and change. The 2009 settlement submission describes places that had already changed, not a landscape kept outside history. Studying a tongkonan connects architecture with skilled work, land, family knowledge and earlier generations. It also shows something useful. A building's importance can reach beyond whoever lives in it, because other people recognise their own relationships in the place.
sections.simpler:
The two photos show certain buildings at certain times. We can see roofs, supports and repeated shapes. The posts and frame are the structure that holds a house up. We can see how the houses stand together. But the photos do not show who lived in each room. They do not show what all Toraja people believe today.

This is living heritage. People still use these places, and they change them. They repair buildings and put in new materials. They decide how traditions go on. A report from 2009 says these villages had already changed. A tongkonan links building skills, land, family and earlier generations. It can matter to many people, not only to the people who live in it.

glossary.definition: Connected with earlier generations of a family or community.
glossary.example: A tongkonan is an ancestral house that links a family with earlier generations.

glossary.definition: The design and building of houses and other places.
glossary.example: Toraja architecture includes houses, rice stores and open spaces between them.

glossary.definition: Decoration that can also carry a meaning.
glossary.example: The carved ornament on a tongkonan can be linked to community rules.

glossary.definition: The parts that hold a building up, and how they fit together.
glossary.example: The posts and beams are part of the house's structure.

glossary.definition: Places and ways of life that people inherit and still use and change.
glossary.example: A tongkonan is living heritage, because families still use and repair it.

write.prompt: Explain one way a tongkonan can show a relationship, not only give shelter. Use the museum's account and one feature you can see. Two or three sentences are enough.
sentenceStarters: One feature I can see is ...
write.example: One feature I can see is the carving on the walls and roof supports of the house in the Rantepao area. The museum explains that some carved designs are linked to social standing and community rules. This shows that a tongkonan can tell people about a family's place in the community, not only keep the rain out. But I cannot tell what each pattern means just from the photo, so I would need to learn more.

sensitiveNotes: Tongkonan are linked with family, customary affairs and ceremonies that communities still keep. Teach them as a community's living practice. No learner is asked to share their own beliefs, family or identity, or to take part in any practice.
educatorNotes: A traditional building is not proof that everyone in a region lives the same way, or that their culture has stopped changing. A Toraja example does not stand for all housing in Indonesia. Keep the pattern a learner can see apart from what a source says it means, and don't invent meanings for carved motifs.

Answer points for Write: an ancestral or family link, family discussion and customary affairs, or carving linked to social standing, connected to a feature a learner can see; the learner keeps the visible pattern apart from the museum's interpretation. Don't require a particular religious belief, or assume all houses today are used the same way.

The settlement description comes from Indonesia's 2009 Tentative List submission, published by UNESCO. It is a proposal by the state, not a World Heritage inscription: don't present the settlements as listed, and don't repeat the submission's dated descriptions of residents.

The Museum Nasional Indonesia account (inventory 16742) is in Indonesian; the reading paraphrases only its form, construction, family and customary uses, and carving. The museum's own collection item is not either pictured building, and its image is not used.

The photographs are two buildings in two places, not before-and-after pictures. Lord Mountbatten is the uploader's Commons username, not the historical person. The Commons records show who took each photograph, when, and under what licence; they are not the source for cultural meaning.
